opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the uncertainty is the most real thing about it. A lot of people want a clean answer, either "AI will take all the jobs" or "it's just another tool, nothing will change much." I don't think either camp actually knows. Nobody does. The capabilities have been moving faster than most of us predicted even two or three years ago, and the way they diffuse into society, into companies, into people's daily work, is even harder to forecast than the technology itself.

So the way I try to think about it is to separate what I can predict from what I can't. I can't predict which specific jobs will exist in ten years. But I can say with some confidence that the ability to learn quickly, to work alongside these systems, and to judge whether their output is actually good will matter more, not less. When the cost of producing something drops close to zero, the scarce thing becomes taste, judgment, and knowing what's worth doing in the first place.

On a personal level, I find it helps not to treat the uncertainty as purely a threat. Uncertainty also means the old paths aren't the only paths anymore. Someone who's twenty-two right now isn't necessarily behind someone who's forty, because a lot of accumulated experience is being re-priced. That's scary if you've invested heavily in one way of doing things, but it's also a kind of opening.

What I do worry about is the transition. Even if things end up fine in aggregate, the people caught in the middle of a fast shift can get hurt, and "it'll work out in the long run" isn't much comfort to them. So I think we should be honest about that rather than just cheerleading. Take the risks seriously, stay curious, keep experimenting with the tools yourself instead of forming opinions from headlines, and try to stay flexible. That's about the best anyone can do right now.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I've stopped trying to resolve the uncertainty, and started trying to live well inside it.

When people ask me "will AI take my job," they're really asking for a forecast, and I think forecasting here is almost a trap. Two years ago I was confident about which tasks would stay human for a long time, and I was wrong about most of them. So the first thing I'd say is: anyone who sounds very certain about what the world looks like in 2030, in either direction, is selling you something, including when it's me.

What I do believe is that the uncertainty isn't evenly distributed. It's not that everything is up in the air. Some things feel quite stable to me. People still need to be understood by other people. Taste, judgment, the ability to decide what's worth doing in the first place, those are getting more valuable, not less, because the cost of execution keeps falling. What's genuinely uncertain is the middle layer, the work that was skilled but mostly about execution, and that's where a lot of people, including a lot of my friends, have built their identities.

So for an individual, I think the useful shift is from "how do I predict this" to "how do I become someone who can absorb surprise." Concretely that means a few things. Keep your fixed costs low, financially and psychologically, so a bad year doesn't break you. Stay close to the tools, because the people who get hurt most are the ones who stop paying attention and then get hit all at once. And invest in relationships and reputation, because those compound regardless of which version of the future arrives.

And then there's the part I find hardest to say on a podcast, which is that some of this anxiety is appropriate. I don't want to perform optimism. There will be people who did everything right and still get displaced, and the honest answer for them is not "learn to adapt," it's that this is a collective problem, and we're going to need policy and institutions that catch people, not just individual grit.

But at the personal level, I keep coming back to a simple thing. Uncertainty about the future has always been the condition. AI just made it loud enough that we can't pretend otherwise anymore. In a strange way, I think that honesty is healthier than the false stability we had before.

astra-6.text:
I think the uncertainty is real, and we should be honest about it. We don’t know exactly which jobs will change, how quickly that will happen, or who will benefit most. But uncertainty doesn’t mean there’s nothing we can do.

I’d separate two questions: What can I do as an individual, and what do we need to do collectively? As an individual, it helps to experiment with AI, understand its limitations, and keep developing your judgment. But we can’t put the entire responsibility on people to constantly reinvent themselves. Institutions and employers also have to help people navigate the transition.

For me, the useful attitude is neither blind optimism nor resignation. It’s being willing to learn while asking hard questions about who gets the benefits and who bears the costs. The future is uncertain partly because the choices that shape it are still being made.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the uncertainty is real, and we should be honest about it. We don’t know exactly how AI will change people’s jobs, opportunities, or sense of purpose. And those changes will affect people differently, so saying “AI will be good for humanity” doesn’t really answer someone who’s worried about their own future.

For me, the useful question is: what can we influence? We can help people learn, give them a voice in how these systems are used, and make sure support is available when their work changes. Individuals can adapt, but they shouldn’t have to carry all the risk themselves.

So I’d stay curious without assuming everything will work out automatically. Uncertainty means there’s room for us to shape the outcome. It also means we need to pay attention to what people are actually experiencing and be willing to change course.
